The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.

# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines.

That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that.

The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. [Control bar](control-bar.md) documents those callbacks and what they replace.

## Board-code form: one label, one submission

BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button.

The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container.

The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group.

On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged.

## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface

Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically.

Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value.

The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform.

A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow.

## Shared control styling

`.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking.

The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX.

`game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen.

## Outcome text is outside the disclosure

The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`.

This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships.

Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations.

## Reflow and review examples

At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport.

A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay.

The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework.

For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order.

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) for the exact validation and React effect. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md).

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. [Offline delivery](../architecture/offline-delivery.md) describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, [Retention policy](retention-policy.md) concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

[Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.

# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [Data exchange policy](../sharing/data-exchange-policy.md) when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

[Preferences store](preferences-store.md) documents the complete aggregate reader. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks

`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.

The object checks are structural, not class checks. `isJsonObject` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` accepts an object if it is non-null and not an array. That helper alone says nothing about which fields are present. The reader supplies the field-specific checks after narrowing the parsed value.

There is a useful asymmetry here. Snapshot validation has an exact-key helper available in the shared format module, but the preference reader does not call it. Extra top-level preference properties are ignored if the fields the reader uses are valid. A successful read returns a freshly constructed `Preferences` value containing only `size` and the validated score map. The current preference format accepts extra top-level properties.

The feature envelope's boundary should not be inferred from that lenience. Its stated outer shape is its own contract. A convenience helper existing nearby does not decide which parser uses it or what a particular version accepts.

## Version labels answer different questions

The project has a product specification version, a preference schema version and explicit interchange format versions. They are not one counter. The current specification identifies itself as 2.2 while the preference discriminator remains 1. A feature envelope uses the numeric version described in its own boundary. A board code's prefix describes its generation algorithm rather than the layout of browser preference JSON.

Keeping those meanings distinct avoids a common support mistake: assuming a newer app release must reject every older saved object. The preferences are accepted according to `PREFERENCES_VERSION` and field validation. The product release number is not read from storage, compared to storage or written into the preference object.

There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.

## A value moves through several representations

It helps to follow one ordinary preference update from the UI rather than treating storage as a single operation. Selecting a different grid size creates a new game. `replaceGame` copies the session preferences and changes `size` to the new board's side length. React renders using that state. The save effect then calls `writePreferences`, which constructs the versioned object, serializes it and passes the string to the supplied store.

The domain state is therefore not the same thing as the serialized object. `Preferences` has no `schemaVersion` field. The writer adds it at the boundary. The reader removes that boundary concern by returning a `Preferences` value with known fields. This is why callers can use `preferences.size` without repeatedly checking a schema version in components.

An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.

## Empty data and invalid data

An empty preference score map is valid. It means no supported size has a saved best in that aggregate. The selected size is still meaningful. By contrast, an absent score-map field, an array in its place, or a map with an impossible score invalidates the preference value. Missing storage and invalid storage reach the same fallback state through different branches.

For a feature collection, an empty array describes a collection with no records. [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) deals with rejection and replacement; it is the place to examine how a failed read interacts with later saving.

Empty data should also be distinguished from unavailable storage. A reader can return an empty state after a denied read, but that return value alone does not prove that the browser is ready to accept a future write. In the preferences API, failure information is intentionally not returned to the caller. The feature failure presentation described in [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) consequently cannot be obtained just by inspecting an empty map.

## Inspecting a captured value

A useful investigation begins with the exact key and original string. A JavaScript object shown after parsing is already one transformation removed from the browser value. Parse failures depend on the text, while field failures depend on the parsed structure. Retaining the original string in an isolated reproduction makes these stages separable.

For preferences, compare the inner `schemaVersion` with `PREFERENCES_VERSION`, then the selected size with `GRID_SIZES`, then each score key and value with the reader's checks. A key spelled `04` is rejected even though converting it to a number yields 4. A score of 7 for a 4x4 board is rejected because eight pairs require at least eight moves. A value can be syntactically valid JSON while failing either of those semantic checks.

For a feature collection, inspect the outer representation before speculating about domain records. A test result for preference JSON is not evidence about feature-record acceptance. Stored values can share a storage mechanism while using different validators.

# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.

# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board.

## What the actions replace

In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns.

`replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event.

The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see [Status bar](status-bar.md) and [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md).

A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes.

## Focus and continuity

Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer.

Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button.

There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work.

## A useful review path

The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`.

These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible.

For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update.

# Corrupt data policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.

`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.

The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.

These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.

## Whole-value validation

The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.

The numeric key must then be supported by `isValidSize`. Each move count must be a nonnegative safe integer, no greater than `MOVES_MAX`, and no smaller than the number of pairs for its size. `MOVES_MAX` is 999999. The lower bound is `numberSize ** 2 / 2`, because completing the board takes at least one move for each pair.

| Side length | Lowest accepted completed move count |
| --- | ---: |
| 4 | 8 |
| 6 | 18 |
| 8 | 32 |
| 10 | 50 |
| 12 | 72 |
| 14 | 98 |
| 16 | 128 |

A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.

This behavior is observable after reload: both the size preference and all previously accepted bests can appear reset when one map entry becomes invalid. It does not indicate that the size failed its own check. [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) explains why the aggregate is read as a unit.

## Examples with different failure causes

This value parses, but its version discriminator is unsupported:

```json
{"schemaVersion":2,"size":6,"bestMoves":{}}
```

This value has the expected version and size, but the score field has the wrong shape:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":[]}
```

This value has a valid map shape and an invalid key spelling:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"04":8}}
```

This value uses a canonical supported key but an impossible completed score:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":7}}
```

All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.

By contrast, this is a valid value with no score for the selected size:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":8}}
```

The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.

## Extra properties and normalization

The preference reader does not enforce an exact property count at the top level. A value with valid expected fields and an additional property can be accepted. The returned application value includes only the selected size and the newly built score map. A normal subsequent write serializes those known fields and the schema discriminator, omitting the extra property.

This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.

The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.

## The timeline of replacement

There are three useful points in a corruption test. Before initialization, the raw store contains the original text. After `readPreferences`, the caller has either accepted preferences or fallback preferences, and the raw store is still unchanged by that function. After `writePreferences`, the store may contain a valid serialized replacement if the write succeeded.

In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.

The simplest way to prove read nonmutation is a store double whose `setItem` records calls. Invoke only `readPreferences`, inspect the original string and check that no write occurred. A separate browser test can demonstrate mount replacement. Combining both assertions into a single post-navigation observation loses the distinction this policy depends on.

## Silent rejection is local to stored preferences

Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.

Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).

None of these parsers establishes authenticity. A manually edited score of 8 for 4x4 is accepted if the surrounding value is valid, even without evidence that eight pairs were played. The constraints establish a plausible stored aggregate, not a verified score history.

## Evidence and useful extensions to a diagnosis

`storage.test.ts` already covers malformed JSON, null, an empty object, unsupported size, scores below the pair count, negative and fractional values, and a noncanonical key. It separately checks that a score at the move cap round-trips and one beyond it is rejected. The browser persistence contract test seeds malformed text before navigation and checks for a playable 16-card default board.

Those tests are focused evidence, not an exhaustive enumeration of every possible JSON string. A new bug report is easiest to isolate with its exact raw value and one field changed at a time. Comparing an independently written valid baseline with the failing value exposes whether the issue concerns syntax, object shape, selected size, key spelling or score bounds. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) gives the browser setup and store doubles for doing that without modifying the source.

# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. [Source layout](source-layout.md) is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, [Architecture](architecture.md) remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.

# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation
