`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.
# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game |
| `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal |
| `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text |
| `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation |
| `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

`storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface.

For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete validation sequence; [Snapshot selection notes](snapshot-selection-notes.md) explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. [Replay format](replay-format.md) explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use [Board code format](board-code-format.md), [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](replay-format.md); for the browser steps around them, use [Sharing FAQ](sharing-faq.md).

# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.2. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.2 | Existing game specification |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.

## A board prefix fixes more than a seed

The reproducibility specification explicitly ties `np1` to the generation algorithm and says that a generation change requires another version. That includes initial paired-face ordering, Park-Miller constants, rejection sampling and backward shuffle order. A different unbiased shuffle is still a different meaning for the same seed.

An implementation refactor that preserves every generated deck leaves that meaning intact. A change that silently produces different cards for an existing code breaks the artifact even if the code still parses. This is the most direct compatibility promise in the exchange model because a short board code appears inside both JSON formats too.

The current `parseBoardCode` supports one prefix. No older-prefix dispatch table, migration helper or multi-version generation registry exists. Future support cannot be assumed from the fact that the prefix contains a digit. [Board code format](board-code-format.md) documents the actual parser and vectors.

## Semantic changes can matter without a new key

A replay's meaning includes advancing time before activation, preserving equal-time array order and resolving a mismatch at its exact closing boundary. Reversing one of those operations would change a version 1 result without changing its object shape. Comparing field lists alone would miss the compatibility effect.

Snapshot meaning includes the lower move bound, the range of pending mismatch time, and the distinction between unstarted and started-zero-move states. Loosening a check can accept objects an older reader rejects. Tightening one can reject previously accepted files. Either observation is more precise than calling the change “validation cleanup”.

Presentation changes have a different scope. Redrawing a face while preserving its numeric matching identity does not alter the generated deck. Changing a visible load notice does not alter accepted JSON. Those changes may need interface or acceptance evidence, but they do not automatically change the exchange format's interpretation.

## What this code does with unsupported data

Snapshot decode returns `null` for an unsupported version; replay read returns the `format` problem. The browser reports its existing generic snapshot failure, while the CLI explains that the file is not a version 1 replay with the exact root fields. Neither tries a best-effort fallback to another version.

There is also no automatic snapshot upgrade on page load. Active progress is not read from local storage. The user explicitly supplies a snapshot through the reproduction controls, and the current decoder accepts or rejects it. Preferences and per-size bests belong to a separate storage contract described in [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md).

The CLI's successful output is version 1 snapshot JSON even though its input is a replay. It does not preserve the replay's actions, and it does not stamp the output with the package release. This conversion can be used as evidence that a replay's interpreted final position is stable across an implementation change.

## Reviewing a proposed change

The useful comparison starts with concrete artifacts. A generation change can be checked against the published seed states and deck. A snapshot change can be checked against an initial position, a one-card position, a pending mismatch and a completed state. A replay change can be checked with equal timestamps, an exact timeout action, ignored activations and an endpoint beyond the elapsed cap.

Those are existing semantic boundaries. They reveal different failure modes: parser acceptance, reconstructed state, action order and output serialization. A test that only checks that JSON parses cannot establish compatibility at the latter three levels.

For an old artifact, ask whether the new reader accepts it and whether it represents the same position or actions. For a new artifact, ask whether the old reader accepts it at all. Exact-key formats often give different answers in those two directions. Recording the direction avoids a vague claim that a change is simply “backward compatible”.

The source currently supplies only single-version readers, not a general migration framework. Any future version handling will need concrete design work at the affected format. The existing boundaries remain the starting evidence: [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md), [Replay format](replay-format.md) and [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md).

# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. [Source layout](source-layout.md) is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, [Architecture](architecture.md) remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.

# Purity guide

This page explains the data-oriented core of Neon Pairs and the practical value of keeping rules independent of rendering and browser effects.

The core receives a board code, state, activation index, logical time amount or serialized text. Its results depend on those inputs. React, storage, event listeners and scheduling enter through adapters. This separation supports browser play and command-line replay with the same transition functions.

## Purity is about observable decisions

`createGame(code)` reconstructs the deck and initializes progress. `activateCard(state, index)` decides whether an activation is ignored, opens one card, matches a pair or creates a mismatch. `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` applies supplied logical time. None needs to know which button was pressed or when a browser timeout was requested.

`isWon(state)` derives victory from matched and deck lengths. `faceUpCards` derives presentation positions from matched positions and selection. These functions avoid a second mutable record of facts that are already available in the state.

The session also contains pure operations. `activateSession` adds feedback and completion preferences to a core transition, while `tickSession` gates a logical advance by generation and pause. Pure does not mean “must be in the top-level game directory”; it means the decision can be evaluated from explicit data without performing an external effect.

## A concrete activation sequence

For `np1-4-1`, positions 2 and 6 both contain face 0. Starting from `createGame`, activating 2 returns a game with `started: true` and a one-card selection. Moves remain zero. Activating 6 returns a game with both positions appended to `matched`, selection closed and moves equal to one.

Activating position 0 and then 1 instead opens a mismatch because the example deck has faces 6 and 7 there. The second activation adds one move and sets `remainingMs` to 800. Activating another position while that mismatch is pending returns the same object.

The same sequence can be used by a pointer journey, a keyboard journey or replay. Their input acquisition differs, but the rule decision does not. A UI-only correction to the move text would leave these other clients inconsistent; a correction in the transition reaches them all.

## Local mutation can produce a pure result

`generateBoard` constructs a local array and swaps elements while generating the seeded deck. That local mutation does not mutate an input deck or expose intermediate state. The completed board description and deck are frozen before return.

Similarly, `readMatched` constructs a local array and map while validating input. Its decision depends on supplied data, and callers do not observe the intermediate accumulation. Purity here does not require expressing every loop as a chain of array combinators.

What matters for shared game state is that transitions do not mutate the state given to them. A new match creates a new matched array; a new selection creates a new selection object. An ignored activation returns the old state. These reference relationships are meaningful to the session commit function and board memoization.

## Readonly types and runtime behavior

The `Board` and `GameState` interfaces expose readonly fields, and arrays are typed readonly. This prevents ordinary TypeScript callers from assigning into them. The generator adds runtime freezing for the board description and deck.

Not every returned progress object is recursively frozen. The code's immutability discipline is expressed through readonly types and functional transitions, with explicit freeze at the stable board boundary. Describing the whole state as deeply frozen at runtime would overstate the implementation.

`faceUpCards` returns a `ReadonlySet<number>` but constructs an ordinary Set internally. The type communicates the consumer contract. `Board` memoizes that derived set rather than storing it in the serialized game. This distinction keeps a convenient rendering index from becoming another authoritative state field.

## Logical time is an argument

`advanceGame` ignores nonfinite or nonpositive deltas and returns unchanged data before start or after victory. For active unfinished games it caps elapsed total and decreases mismatch remainder. An advance that expires a mismatch closes selection in the same call.

Replay uses this property by advancing from the previous timestamp to the next action before activating. Equal timestamps produce a zero advance and preserve array order. A timeout boundary is therefore a numerical question that can be tested without waiting for browser scheduling.

The browser controller supplies measured active deltas through the session clock. Its effect lifecycle determines which intervals are active. The core does not infer hidden periods from a timestamp history or attempt to compensate for browser throttling itself. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the adapter side.

## Validation is a pure boundary too

Serialized text is untrusted input even when produced by another copy of the game. `parseJson` returns unknown data or an undefined malformed marker. `isJsonObject`, integer checks and exact-key checks narrow it before any state is installed.

The snapshot decoder checks the code, bounds, matched positions and selection against a newly reconstructed deck. It checks a minimum move count and whether an unstarted state contains impossible progress. A valid result is a new `GameState`; an invalid result is null. A failed decode does not partially modify the current browser game.

This validation is structural and domain-specific, not a reconstruction of every possible prior activation history. For example, the decoder checks lower bounds on moves and relationships between start state and progress; it does not replay a missing action log to prove that a particular elapsed value occurred. The format contains a state, not that history.

`saved-format.ts` uses `TextEncoder` to measure UTF-8 bytes. This is a standard facility available in both the browser and the Node environments used here. It does not read browser state, storage or the DOM. Treating every standard host-provided constructor as a browser effect would obscure the actual independence these modules need.

## Invalid arguments have explicit outcomes

Different APIs serve different callers. `boardCode` and `generateBoard` throw on invalid board descriptions because their constructors expect a valid input. `parseBoardCode` returns null, providing a nonthrowing validation boundary. `decodeSnapshot` and `replayGame` return null for invalid text, while `readReplay` exposes a structured problem.

`activateCard` instead ignores invalid indices and illegal attempts by returning its input state. That is suitable for the activation path, where stale or repeated input should not corrupt progress. `advanceGame` similarly ignores unsuitable amounts and inactive states.

These are existing contracts, not a universal rule that pure functions never throw. A function can be deterministic and still reject an argument with an exception. The important review question is whether its caller expects an exception, a null result, a problem value or unchanged state.

## Small shared helpers have real clients

`saved-format.ts` holds object narrowing, safe nonnegative integer checks, exact-key matching, byte measurement and JSON parsing. Snapshot, replay and preference validation actually share those operations. Their domain checks remain in their own modules.

A helper such as `isNonnegativeSafeInteger` cannot by itself decide whether a number is a legal move count. Snapshot adds the move cap and consistency lower bound; preferences add the board's minimum completed moves; replay uses it for timestamps and positions before applying its own range checks.

Keeping those checks explicit prevents a superficially reusable “validate number” abstraction from hiding different meanings. The architecture specification asks for shared support when two real behaviors need the same meaning, and the current helper file is small enough to inspect against its callers.

## Rendering consumes outcomes

Components derive visible state from the returned game rather than reading classes back into the rules. Focus stays in the board, and storage writes follow preference decisions through a hook. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) and [Session module](session-module.md) explain those adapters.

## Evidence made possible by this shape

Literal decks, direct transition tests, malformed-format cases and numerical clock steps can be checked without rendering. Browser journeys then address native input, focus, storage and delivery. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains why these are complementary forms of evidence.

## Reviewing an accidental effect

A rule that imports a component, reads a DOM element or performs storage access would bring environment state into a computation currently driven by arguments. The source audit scans selected core filenames for known effect markers, but its list and regular expressions are limited. Reading the imports and operations remains part of review.

A less obvious problem is mutating an input array while returning a new outer object. That can preserve or corrupt references in ways memoized consumers do not expect. The existing transitions instead create changed collections where their meanings change and keep stable collections where they do not.

A useful explanation of a core change can therefore state its input, output, ignored cases and retained references. If that explanation requires a mounted component to define the result, it is probably describing an adapter concern or an incomplete rule boundary. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) connects that distinction to file placement.

# Test policy

This page explains the verification layers used by Neon Pairs and the kinds of failures each layer can establish.

The repository checks rule transitions, serialized input, source conventions and complete browser journeys. These checks share documented examples but do not all run in the same environment. `npm test` runs Vitest; `npm run test:e2e` builds the current application and diagnostic entries, then uses Node's test runner with Playwright browser support.

## Focused evidence stays near behavior

The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.

Adjacency is useful because a transition and its evidence can be read in one pass. It does not mean every production file in the repository has a one-to-one test file. Some concerns have several focused files: completion, move limits, snapshot selection and replay ordering each get separate attention. Other helpers are exercised through a broader behavior or browser journey.

The architecture specification A10 asks for focused tests near behavior, independent literal generation vectors, transitions checked against stated rules and built HTML checked from disk as well as served. Those are different obligations because no single test environment can establish all of them.

## What Vitest includes

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. It does not include the browser files in `tests`, which end in `.e2e.test.ts` and run under the separate command. There is no hidden browser suite behind `npm test`.

Most unit tests use `node:assert/strict` with `test` imported from Vitest. They call pure functions directly. Clock arithmetic receives numerical observations; session transitions receive a session object; preference tests pass a memory or failing store. This makes failures specific: a mismatch boundary can be checked without waiting for a real timeout.

The script tests also run here. `replay.test.ts` launches child processes to exercise command output and failure exits, and the source-audit files read authored files and configuration. The CLI test has a 60-second timeout because child processes can be slow on a busy verifier. That allowance is test scheduling, not a game timing constant.

## Independence for generated data

A generator test that computes its expected deck using the same generator can prove little about compatibility. The repository instead contains a literal example deck for `np1-4-1`, initial recurrence values and independent rejection vectors. Browser support also has `specDeal` in `tests/deal-oracle.ts`, which expresses the shuffle with BigInt arithmetic.

The rejection tests cover both a draw above the accepted limit and a draw exactly at it. That equality case matters because a one-character comparison change would alter the seeded result. Completion tests iterate supported grid sizes and activate every actual pair to prove that each generated board can finish with one move per pair.

The literal fixture and oracle serve different purposes. A literal fixes a public example. An independent implementation can check more combinations but can still share a mistaken interpretation of the written rule. The documented format, literal vectors and independent arithmetic together provide stronger evidence than any one of them alone.

## State transitions and identity

`activateCard` returns the same state object for ignored input: an invalid index, a matched position, the already revealed first card or input during a mismatch. Tests can check both the unchanged values and reference identity. Identity matters because the session controller and memoized presentation use it to avoid unnecessary work.

A successful first activation changes `started` and selection without adding a move. A second distinct activation adds one move and either matches immediately or opens a mismatch. The rule tests can check this without going through pointer events. Browser journeys then establish that actual buttons call that same path.

The cap tests cover continued matching and victory at `MOVES_MAX = 999_999`, and elapsed-time tests cover the total cap. A limit on the number displayed or serialized is not evidence that play should terminate there. The meaningful regression is whether ordinary transitions still work at the boundary.

## Format validation evidence

Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.

Replay tests add ordering and action count constraints. Equal timestamps preserve array order, while logical time advances before each activation. `replay-order.test.ts` checks a same-time third activation blocked by the preceding mismatch. These are rules about accepted actions, not browser task order.

Round trips establish that the serializer and decoder agree on valid states, but rejection cases are necessary because both could otherwise agree on an overly permissive format. The repository's exact-key helpers and validators make those cases inspectable. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) provide the product-facing definitions.

## Browser command and fresh output

The end-to-end script is:

```sh
npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 "tests/*.e2e.test.ts"
```

The production build type checks first. Both build stages precede the test runner with `&&`, so a failure prevents the suite from opening an older output. `build:art` creates the face sheet and the session harness separately from `dist/index.html`.

The browser wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts` creates a new context per journey and registers its closure with the Node test context. It collects page errors and asserts that none occurred after a successful journey body. It creates an artifact directory from the test name and restricts output paths to a filename. A shared browser and local server are closed in the file-level teardown.

The standard journey timeout is 30 seconds and the long one is 90 seconds. Playwright assertions use a 15-second configured timeout. These values make verification tolerant of busy machines; they do not lengthen the logical mismatch interval, which controlled-clock tests exercise precisely.

## Disk and HTTP evidence

`tests/game-fixture.ts` defines a `file:` URL for the distribution and separate URLs for the two diagnostic builds. `tests/artifact-server.ts` also serves the built HTML on an ephemeral loopback port, accepting only `/`. This is a test server around the finished file, not the Vite development server.

Disk delivery demonstrates that the HTML carries its own code and assets. HTTP-origin journeys establish preference persistence in a browser environment with a stable storage origin for the journey. A result from one mode does not establish the other, because storage behavior on local files varies.

`build-output.e2e.test.ts` reads the HTML and checks for the excluded fetch and module-preload markers. Browser journeys can additionally watch requests. Source inspection, artifact inspection and actual browser behavior contribute different evidence about offline delivery. [Offline delivery](offline-delivery.md) explains why all three are useful.

## Browser interactions that pure tests cannot see

Arrow navigation tests can check the helper's target arithmetic directly, but only the browser can show where focus lands, whether Tab leaves and whether scrolling keeps the focus ring visible. Native click behavior also matters for keyboard activation, context menus and touch scrolling. The card component uses the native click path rather than a separate game action per input method.

Artwork tests render all 128 faces through the real `Card` component in the separate face sheet. Layout journeys cover large boards, visible scrollbars, zoom and touch. Accessibility journeys inspect the Chromium accessibility tree through a complete keyboard interaction. The README explicitly separates this tree evidence from a spoken screen-reader acceptance journey.

These distinctions prevent overclaiming. A passing tree check does not mean a human has listened to every announcement. A passing layout measurement does not mean every browser family has been tested. [Browser support](../quality/browser-support.md) and [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) are the related places for that evidence.

## Time and lifecycle regressions

The clock tests are intentionally layered. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks arithmetic, while `session.test.ts` checks stale generations and paused state. Browser files exercise hidden intervals, idle pause periods, fractional observations and exports between timer callbacks.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` overrides the observed clock and sends an overdue click in the same browser task. No scheduled timer can run first, so this isolates the controller's synchronize-before-activate behavior. `idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` avoids inspecting the game repeatedly during inactivity, exposing bugs that an incidental export synchronization could otherwise mask.

The session harness makes teardown observable by unmounting the actual game. `timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timers and visibility listeners, checks that one active timer exists, then checks cleanup after unmount. It also follows an earlier mismatch with a later mismatch in the same deal. This catches mistakes that merely changing the deal generation would not expose.

## Source and runtime records

[Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) records the package, compiler, source and naming patterns inspected by the static checks. Browser setup separately writes its observed runtime versions and can enforce the named combination. These records describe different evidence; neither replaces a behavior test.

For a review, the useful account names the changed behavior and the check that observes it. [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) gives examples of that mapping.

# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls `useGame`, passes session values and controller actions into the UI, and imports `game.css`. Its output is a single main element containing the heading, instructions, deal controls, statistics, turn feedback, board and reproduction controls.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
