The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker. No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices. ## Timing questions exposed by an overlay A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source. Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model. Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection. The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics. ## Focus ownership Opening the confirmation establishes a temporary interaction context. The policy above states its initial focus and cancellation result. That avoids relying on DOM order alone to make the safe continuation choice the first keyboard target. After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation. A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility. The board also remembers focus independently of actual focus. Opening another surface would not, by itself, mean its last card index should become a selected turn. A player returning to the board still needs the distinction between orientation and activation described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md). ## Review notes for a proposed implementation The most useful review evidence separates opening, continuing and leaving. A single screenshot of the open surface cannot establish which element is focused, whether Escape follows the continuation path, or whether the underlying controller already replaced the game before a decision. A source trace can identify the first state-changing call relative to the decision. A keyboard trace can identify the active element at opening and after cancellation. A populated game, especially one with a pending mismatch, makes unintended early replacement visible. These are ways of observing the stated policy and existing game lifecycle, rather than additional product requirements. Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus. The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle. # Error display guide This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game. The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available. ## The visible location Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body. Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence. Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width. The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system. ## Who decides that a load failed BoardCodeForm reads its draft through FormData and calls the `loadBoard` prop. The controller in `use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace and checks `parseBoardCode`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidBoard)` and returns false before clock reset or replacement. Reproduction passes the complete snapshot draft to `loadSnapshot`. The controller calls `decodeSnapshot`. Failure calls `notice(SessionNotice.invalidSnapshot)` and returns false, again before resetting or replacing the game. The textarea component does not try to validate JSON structure itself. `SessionNotice` in `session.ts` owns the literal messages. The shared `notice` helper sets both `feedback` and `loadNotice` and advances announcement identity. The exact words therefore come from the session boundary that knows the operation failed, rather than being duplicated in each field's change handler. This ordering is important. If a load reset the timer before parsing, even an invalid draft could alter play. If it replaced the game before reporting failure, the notice would not describe the preservation behavior promised by the controls specification. The current callbacks validate first. ## What a failure preserves A failed board-code load leaves the input's DOM node intact because generation does not change. Its edited value remains available. A failed snapshot load leaves Reproduction's local string state intact. Neither failure clears the draft to make the panel look clean. The game object, board size, matched positions, selection, moves and elapsed state are not replaced by the error path. The existing game can continue to advance active time. An invalid input is not an imported pause, and it does not freeze a pending mismatch merely because a notice appeared. Focus memory also survives because Board is not remounted. A player who last visited a far card can return there after correcting a form. The current saved size is unchanged by a failed load; successful replacement is what updates that preference. The load notice is a session field separate from the game. Adding it can produce a render without changing card state. This is why comparing the complete session object for identity is different from asserting that gameplay was replaced. [Game state model](../gameplay/game-state-model.md) and [Session module](../architecture/session-module.md) explain those boundaries. ## Focus depends on how submission began A click on Load board ordinarily leaves focus on the button. If the code is invalid, BoardCodeForm does not issue another focus call. A keyboard Enter submission from inside Board code leaves focus in the field on failure, so the user can continue editing. On successful Enter submission, the input is about to be replaced because it is keyed by generation. BoardCodeForm explicitly focuses its Load board ref when the callback returns true. That is a success-path focus correction, not an error-summary jump. Load snapshot is a `type="button"` action. Its handler passes local text to the controller and does not move focus elsewhere on failure or success. The snapshot textarea stays mounted. Export likewise keeps its action focus and fills the field rather than focusing or selecting it automatically. These cases show why “errors focus the field” would be an inaccurate description of this interface. The source preserves the user's current interaction where it can. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers the complete set of current focus transfers. ## Notices are outcomes, not sticky field annotations `loadNotice` is one session string used for the latest published load outcome. It is not an error object keyed separately by field. The UI does not render two simultaneous field-specific error paragraphs or an error list above the panel. After an invalid Board code attempt followed by an invalid snapshot attempt, the visible notice is the snapshot message. The Board code draft can still be invalid; the notice records the most recent action rather than continuously describing all field values. Editing the snapshot string changes local state but does not itself clear the controller's notice. Editing Board code is native uncontrolled editing and likewise does not call a notice-clearing function. The outcome can remain visible while the user works on a correction. Export replaces textarea text but does not explicitly clear `loadNotice`. Card turns update feedback without rewriting the load notice. New Game, Restart and a successful board-code replacement clear both through `replaceGame(..., false)`. Successful snapshot loading replaces the notice with its load outcome, and Resume clears it when continuing play. This lifecycle explains a report that an old load message is still visible after editing. The message is action feedback, not a live validator attached to every keystroke. Adding an on-change clearing behavior would be a change to this lifecycle, not a fix to a missing CSS state. ## Format validity is more than native limits Board code has a 32-character entry cap, but many shorter strings are invalid. An unsupported size, zero seed, leading zeros or malformed separators fail the parser even when the input is well below its native maximum. The loader's surrounding trim is a deliberate adapter step, not broad syntax repair. Snapshot JSON has a 65536-character textarea limit and a UTF-8 byte bound in the decoder. Malformed JSON is only one failure kind. Unsupported versions, unknown properties, inconsistent matched positions, invalid selections and out-of-range counters can also produce the same UI error. The UI intentionally gives the short outcome rather than exposing the decoder's internal reasoning. There is no implemented per-property error report or highlighted JSON line number. [Import safety policy](../sharing/import-safety-policy.md) and [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) are the useful debugging references for engineers handling a rejected draft. A completed valid snapshot is not an error merely because its result exceeds the local stored best. It loads as completed with a completion notice and static banner. An unfinished valid snapshot loads paused with an instruction to resume. The notice area carries both success and failure outcomes, so `.load-notice` is a more accurate name than a field-specific error class. ## Existing visual and semantic treatment The notice paragraph uses the surrounding document styles and the load-status layout. The current fields do not receive `aria-invalid`, an error border class or an inline replacement label on failure. Those absences are part of the existing markup, not evidence that validation did not run. The paragraph can wrap and has `min-width: 0` in its flex row. Resume can wrap alongside it on a constrained viewport. There is no absolute positioning that places a message over the field. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explains how the notice row relates to the grid inside the disclosure. Name-related errors do not exist in the current component tree. Their policies are in [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The load forms use their own messages and have no shared name-error component. ## Evidence for preservation and retry `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` populates progress, submits both invalid drafts and compares exported state before and after. It also advances the browser clock to show that the preserved game is still running. That distinguishes failure preservation from an accidental reset or pause. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` submits a valid code with Enter, then an invalid code, checking both focus and the unchanged card count. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` checks exact notices, retained drafts and action focus. Repeated invalid submissions are covered in the announcement and accessibility journeys. A useful defect report includes the draft, action origin, notice text and a before/after state observation. For example, an invalid snapshot followed by an unchanged exported selection is evidence of preservation. A notice alone cannot prove it, and a preserved game alone cannot prove that the user was told what happened. Reviewing both gives the error path its full meaning. # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet # Competition results and local records This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs. The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences. ## The competition boundary A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board. For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other. The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time. ## What the game saves today `src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values. An example stored value is: ```json { "schemaVersion": 1, "size": 10, "bestMoves": { "4": 12, "6": 24 } } ``` There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide. The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history. [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format. ## Two ordinary paths have side effects The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game. The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object. Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game. There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller. ## Where saving actually happens `useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted. Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize. The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload. `rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) cover those existing responsibilities. ## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best. That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path. `src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot. ## A concrete review example Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8. The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result. A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen. The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

# ADR 019: Use a custom confirmation overlay

This historical record explains the retired div-based confirmation overlay and its original interaction model.

Status: Superseded by [Dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md)

## Original context

The early interface discussion included actions that might discard an in-progress choice. A confirmation was intended to keep the player from accidentally losing work while preserving the visible board underneath. At the time, the team chose a custom overlay because it appeared easy to style consistently with the dark panel and card surfaces.

The old decision used a div overlay with `role="alertdialog"`, a focus trap written by hand and two buttons labeled Cancel and Discard. The overlay covered the page while keeping the underlying state in memory. This record describes that historical design; the replacement policy governs current dialog decisions.

## Decision as originally made

Cancel dismissed the confirmation and returned the player to the interrupted activity. Discard accepted the pending destructive intent. The overlay did not itself own the game rules; it held the user's choice about whether the initiating action should proceed. That distinction was meant to avoid modifying the board and then attempting to undo it on cancellation.

The custom trap moved Tab and Shift+Tab among the confirmation's controls. The dialog role and accessible name were intended to make the interruption understandable to assistive technology. Returning focus to the initiating control was part of the original interaction sketch, because leaving focus on a removed overlay would make the next keyboard step unpredictable.

## Reasoning at the time

A div-based overlay allowed the same border, background and spacing choices as the rest of the page. It could be rendered conditionally with React without invoking a browser dialog method. The team expected that only two buttons and a short message would make the focus logic manageable.

An inline confirmation would have avoided trapping focus but would have competed with the board and controls for space. A browser-native confirmation prompt offered limited presentation control. The custom overlay seemed to give a clear pause in the interaction without introducing a separate screen or route.

## Costs that were easy to underestimate

A focus trap is more than cycling between the first and last button in a static example. Controls can be removed, disabled or focused programmatically. Background content must not remain an alternate interaction path. Escape and dismissal behavior need coherent ownership. Styling an overlay is straightforward; duplicating browser dialog behavior consistently is a larger maintenance burden.

The small number of visible controls did not remove these responsibilities. It merely made the first prototype look complete before keyboard, assistive-technology and interrupted-render cases had been explored. The prototype underestimated the maintenance burden of the custom trap.

## Relationship to the present game

`Game.tsx` composes the status, board, controls and reproduction panel directly. Its current new-deal and restart paths do not mount the historical overlay. Reproduction uses a native disclosure, and importing progress uses a session pause with Resume.

[Dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) is the replacement authority. This record supplies historical context for discussions about confirmation behavior and explains why a custom trap may appear in old notes. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md), [ADR 006](adr-006-native-controls.md) and [ADR 043](adr-043-keyboard-parity.md) cover the related concerns without reviving the retired approach.

# ADR 019: Use a custom confirmation overlay

This historical record explains the retired div-based confirmation overlay and its original interaction model.

Status: Superseded by [Dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md)

## Original context

The early interface discussion included actions that might discard an in-progress choice. A confirmation was intended to keep the player from accidentally losing work while preserving the visible board underneath. At the time, the team chose a custom overlay because it appeared easy to style consistently with the dark panel and card surfaces.

The old decision used a div overlay with `role="alertdialog"`, a focus trap written by hand and two buttons labeled Cancel and Discard. The overlay covered the page while keeping the underlying state in memory. This record describes that historical design; the replacement policy governs current dialog decisions.

## Decision as originally made

Cancel dismissed the confirmation and returned the player to the interrupted activity. Discard accepted the pending destructive intent. The overlay did not itself own the game rules; it held the user's choice about whether the initiating action should proceed. That distinction was meant to avoid modifying the board and then attempting to undo it on cancellation.

The custom trap moved Tab and Shift+Tab among the confirmation's controls. The dialog role and accessible name were intended to make the interruption understandable to assistive technology. Returning focus to the initiating control was part of the original interaction sketch, because leaving focus on a removed overlay would make the next keyboard step unpredictable.

## Reasoning at the time

A div-based overlay allowed the same border, background and spacing choices as the rest of the page. It could be rendered conditionally with React without invoking a browser dialog method. The team expected that only two buttons and a short message would make the focus logic manageable.

An inline confirmation would have avoided trapping focus but would have competed with the board and controls for space. A browser-native confirmation prompt offered limited presentation control. The custom overlay seemed to give a clear pause in the interaction without introducing a separate screen or route.

## Costs that were easy to underestimate

A focus trap is more than cycling between the first and last button in a static example. Controls can be removed, disabled or focused programmatically. Background content must not remain an alternate interaction path. Escape and dismissal behavior need coherent ownership. Styling an overlay is straightforward; duplicating browser dialog behavior consistently is a larger maintenance burden.

The small number of visible controls did not remove these responsibilities. It merely made the first prototype look complete before keyboard, assistive-technology and interrupted-render cases had been explored. The prototype underestimated the maintenance burden of the custom trap.

## Relationship to the present game

`Game.tsx` composes the status, board, controls and reproduction panel directly. Its current new-deal and restart paths do not mount the historical overlay. Reproduction uses a native disclosure, and importing progress uses a session pause with Resume.

[Dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) is the replacement authority. This record supplies historical context for discussions about confirmation behavior and explains why a custom trap may appear in old notes. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md), [ADR 006](adr-006-native-controls.md) and [ADR 043](adr-043-keyboard-parity.md) cover the related concerns without reviving the retired approach.

A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:33:No dialog state exists in `Session`. Its fields are `game`, `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. The existing `paused` flag specifically represents unfinished snapshot import. Reusing that flag for a new overlay without considering its other consumers would also affect Resume and load notices.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:37:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:41:Replacement does have a well-defined lifecycle today. `clock.reset()` and the session generation prevent old pending updates from affecting a replacement game. If a leave decision leads to that existing path, stale-timer protection still belongs to the session. The dialog does not need to know the two selected card indices to implement that protection.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:49:After a decision, the durability of the source control matters. Existing action buttons generally remain mounted after a deal replacement, while Resume removes itself. Game handles Resume by moving focus before the button is removed. That is a concrete example of a disappearing source, though it is not a dialog implementation.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:51:A leave feature may keep or remove its trigger as part of its surrounding screen. Its focus return depends on which controls remain mounted. A review can inspect the final active element and its visibility.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:61:Current browser tests establish focus retention on ordinary buttons, invalid draft preservation, Resume's transfer order and stale-timer protection. They do not establish a dialog journey. Any future report of dialog coverage has to point at the corresponding implementation and evidence, rather than citing those tests because they also involve focus.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:63:The relevant background is [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) for element choice, [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for page orientation and [New game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) for the existing replacement boundary. Together they make it possible to review a concrete leave interaction alongside the existing game lifecycle.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:28:The function returns the current index for an arrow at an edge rather than returning null. That still counts as a handled arrow. The hook prevents its default behavior, then attempts to focus the same card. A key with no movement target is a different case: null means the board leaves it to the browser.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:30:## Keys the board leaves alone
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:34:The event handler only calls `preventDefault()` when the result is non-null. This is the mechanism that preserves browser shortcuts such as Alt+ArrowLeft and Ctrl+End. It also leaves Shift+Tab to ordinary reverse traversal. The board does not intercept all keydowns and then try to recreate the browser's behavior for a selected subset.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:44:This is a memory of focus, not of a selected game card. A player can reveal index 0, arrow to index 5 without revealing it, leave with Tab and return to index 5. The game may still have index 0 as its only unmatched revealed card. Collapsing those two kinds of state would make exploratory movement change play.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:54:A regular turn, mismatch closure or clock render does not replace that key. The remembered location survives those updates. So does opening or closing the reproduction details element, which is outside the Board. A failed load leaves the generation unchanged and does not reset navigation memory.
docs/interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md:72:The helper leaves page scrolling to the browser. It does not freeze the outer document or always force the board to its top-left corner. Nearest means making the card visible with a small necessary movement, rather than centering every visited card. Tests check interior cards as well as corners because padding alone can hide a mid-board outline problem.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:16:The current page has no name editor, dialog or result table. A change introducing one has more scope than styling an existing control. Its relevant policy is linked below, and its current behavior has to be established from its own implementation.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:24:- Both actions reset selection, pairs, moves and elapsed time, and leave their action button focused.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:30:The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records that separate feature boundary.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:64:- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:69:- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a simple, clear communicator. You keep your own judgment, disagree when you have reason, and reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

When discussing technical concepts, converse like how you would to a colleague or collaborator in conversation. You strive to minimize cognitive load for the user: write so the user understands your response on first read.

Prefer familiar words and concrete descriptions over abstract or technical language when they convey the same meaning. Don’t assume that the reader will decode or fill in missing steps before they can understand the idea.

Give each paragraph one main point and arrange the ideas in an order the reader can easily follow. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits.

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:"/"Significance:"/"Perspective:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer.", "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely". Avoid hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives.

State the intended action directly. Do not add what you won't do, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "it is about X, not about Y", "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless explicit authorization is already provided.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

You can use the `functions.send_user_message_async` or `functions.request_user_input_async` tool (depending on which is available) to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. # Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.
# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

## Documentation map

Every project document, by area. Project-wide policies apply to all new work, including work that doesn't mention them.

### Gameplay

- [rules.md](gameplay/rules.md): Card matching, moves, timing and victory rules
- [deck-generation.md](gameplay/deck-generation.md): Board-code parsing, paired deck construction, deterministic shuffle arithmetic, and fresh seed selection.
- [selection-state.md](gameplay/selection-state.md): The closed, one-card, and mismatch selection alternatives, visibility, and decoding boundaries.
- [turn-resolution.md](gameplay/turn-resolution.md): Activation guards, second-reveal resolution, and the ordering of time, feedback, and turns.
- [scoring-and-moves.md](gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md): Pair progress, move accounting, minimum completions, and continued play at the move cap.
- [best-score-records.md](gameplay/best-score-records.md): Per-size best move comparison, preference validation, persistence, and imported-completion behavior.
- [board-size-catalogue.md](gameplay/board-size-catalogue.md): The seven board sizes, exact card and pair counts, included faces, and size selection behavior.
- [win-conditions.md](gameplay/win-conditions.md): Full matched coverage, the final transition, stopped time, and played versus imported completion.
- [game-state-model.md](gameplay/game-state-model.md): GameState fields, invariants, derived values, immutable transitions, and session boundaries.
- [pair-identity.md](gameplay/pair-identity.md): Position indices versus face numbers, artwork identity dimensions, and hidden-face rendering.
- [mismatch-interval.md](gameplay/mismatch-interval.md): The exact 800-millisecond active interval, synchronization, pauses, and stale timer protection.
- [elapsed-time-rules.md](gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md): Active-time accumulation, browser observations, display conversion, caps, and snapshot precision.
- [new-game-and-restart.md](gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md): What fresh deals, repeats, size changes, loads, Resume, exports, and reloads preserve or reset.
- [gameplay-faq.md](gameplay/gameplay-faq.md): Answers to common play and maintenance questions, with links to detailed behavior pages.

# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md) explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.

[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a memory game that runs offline from one HTML file and keeps local best moves for each board size.

You can repeat a deal with its board code, save progress as a snapshot or run timed actions through the replay command.

Status: implements product spec version 2.2.

## Install

Use the named test combination, Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0 and Playwright 1.64.1 with Chromium 156.0.8078.4. From this folder, install the locked tools:

```powershell
npm ci --cache .npm-cache
```

Chromium 156.0.8078.4 comes with the project's image, so browser tests need no download. Browser tests use fresh contexts. They stop their browser and local HTTP server when they finish.

## Play

Run `npm run build`, then open `dist/index.html` from disk. The game makes no network requests. To keep saved sizes and scores on a stable HTTP origin, run `npm run dev`. Stop it when you finish.

Use Grid size to choose a board. Reveal two cards with a click, tap, Enter or Space. Arrow keys move board focus. Other keys stay with the browser. Tab leaves the board. New Game gives another deal. Restart repeats the current deal.

Open Reproduce a game to load a board code or export progress. Loading an unfinished snapshot pauses it. Resume returns focus to the remembered card and continues the remaining mismatch interval. A completed snapshot loads as completed without Resume. Elapsed time stops at 359999999ms while play continues. The minutes and seconds display reaches 5999:59. Moves stop at 999999. Matching and victory continue at that count. Saved bests use the same move limit.

## Replay

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` with a version 1 replay JSON file. Valid input prints only its final version 1 snapshot JSON to stdout and exits 0. Invalid input prints nothing to stdout, writes a message to stderr and exits nonzero. The command's silent flag suppresses its npm banner so stdout stays JSON. Other npm commands keep their errors and warnings. Replay timestamps can reach the safe integer limit. Elapsed time uses the same cap as browser play.

## Check

Run the checks from this folder:

```powershell
npm run typecheck
npm test
$env:NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION = '1'
npm run test:e2e
npm run format:check
```

`npm test` runs the unit and static checks with Vitest 5.0.5. `test:e2e` type checks and builds current source before opening the new HTML. It also builds the face sheet and session harness as separate diagnostic entries. The game distribution contains no diagnostic entry.

The browser command writes the Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium versions it ran on to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`. With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` set to `1`, it also fails unless they match the named combination. Use the flag for named-combination evidence. Other supported runtimes, such as Node 24.19, run without it.

The locked install, type check, Vitest unit tests, build from current source and Chromium journeys have passed on the named combination with the flag set. Other versions have no test record here.

## Accessibility

Keyboard, card names, atomic turn feedback, reduced motion, touch scrolling and the equivalent zoom layout at 640x400 CSS pixels with device scale 2 have browser checks. The diagnostic face sheet draws all 128 faces at 44px.

Playwright checks Chromium's accessibility tree through a complete keyboard journey. It checks controls, card names, states, turn results, the final summary, Tab exit and New Game. The developer provides this tree evidence and the tool record. You confirm spoken output during acceptance with your screen reader.

Tree record: Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1. Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.

Delivered projects from document setups keep the product specification in `docs/`.

Follow the requirements in docs/ for this project.
# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture
